stem:
A 32-year-old man with known epilepsy ran out of levetiracetam three days ago. In the emergency department he has a generalised tonic–clonic seizure. IV midazolam was given at 5 minutes and repeated at 10 minutes, and the seizure is still continuing at 15 minutes. His airway is supported with oxygen (SpO₂ 93%), bedside glucose is 6.1 mmol/L (reference 4.0–7.8) and an IV cannula is in place.

What should be given next?

options.label: A
options.text: A third dose of IV midazolam
options.explanation: Two doses is the usual limit; more benzodiazepine increases respiratory depression and hypotension without much extra seizure control.

options.label: B
options.text: An IV loading dose of levetiracetam
options.explanation: Benzodiazepines are first-line, but after two doses further doses add respiratory depression for little extra effect. A seizure continuing after them is established status epilepticus, treated with an IV second-line agent: levetiracetam, phenytoin or valproate are similarly effective, and levetiracetam also replaces his missed medicine.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Anaesthesia and intubation are for refractory status after a second-line drug has failed, or for airway failure; his oxygenation is being maintained.

options.label: D
options.text: Glucose 50% and thiamine before any drug
options.explanation: His glucose has been checked and is normal, so giving glucose delays effective treatment.

options.label: E
options.text: His usual levetiracetam via nasogastric tube
options.explanation: Enteral absorption is too slow and unreliable in a convulsing patient; established status needs an IV loading dose.

context: Convulsive status epilepticus: a benzodiazepine first (up to two doses), then an IV second-line agent such as levetiracetam, phenytoin or valproate, with anaesthesia for refractory seizures.
